rationale: A wins because it finds four actual stories at four different altitudes, not just three ways to admire the same pricing fact. Its "Rivian's new stalls will speak both plugs — CCS and NACS on every one" is a clean infrastructure-trade angle B bizarrely throws away as "duplicate." B has one strong finance angle, but "Rivian charges rival-brand drivers more than its own" and "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates" are basically the same coin flipped over.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief: a proprietary fast-charging network is a moat" is a strong lens, but it is external context, not in the supplied facts; it needs sourcing before it carries a contrarian pitch.
"with no automaker partnership to force its hand" leans past the fact block. The update says no partnership was announced, not that none exists or none influenced the move.
"Every other EV driver just gained 3,500 fast chargers" is punchy but a little too totalizing until connector compatibility, geography, and app/session mechanics are nailed down.
gaps_in_B: "The infrastructure angle on Rivian opening its network" as a refused "duplicate" is the big miss. The CCS-plus-NACS commitment is a separate infrastructure design story, not a rewrap of open access.
"Rivian charges rival-brand drivers more than its own" and "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates" split one pricing fact into two angles. That is padding with better shoes.
"Tesla Supercharger access, Electrify America, the NACS transition" imports outside comparators not supplied in the update. Usable with sourcing, sloppy as given.

"whether discounted charging becomes a retention lever the way it has for one walled competitor" invents a retention comparison the facts do not support. That is exactly how a decent angle gets infected.
